topic: job search tracking, application tailoring, and interview prep
segment: career changers and laid-off tech workers
blind_spots: No interview-preparation evidence addresses practice interviews, question generation, feedback quality, anxiety, scheduling, coding practice, or offer negotiation.
There is little segmentation by geography, industry, seniority, disability, age, or employment status beyond tech workers and students.
Several items are headlines, questions, marketing-style claims, or service offers rather than detailed first-person accounts of pain.
The evidence does not define the unit behind Huntr's 'median sat in the high 60s,' so its magnitude cannot be interpreted precisely.
No evidence measures how widespread the filtering, note-taking, networking, or app-reliability problems are.
No outcome data shows whether resume tailoring, AI-generated resumes, manual application assistance, or cover letters improve interview or hiring rates.
No evidence directly evaluates dedicated job-search trackers, status pipelines, reminders, follow-up scheduling, duplicate detection, or cross-platform application history.
The Dice review has no date, and the Glassdoor reliability quote appears to originate in 2020 despite the evidence entry being dated 2026.
contradictions: The market is explicitly heterogeneous: it 'still works fast for some' while being 'grindingly slow for others,' so prolonged searches are not universal.
One item questions whether tailoring every resume makes a big difference, while other items promote rapid AI tailoring or ATS tailoring services; the evidence does not resolve effectiveness.

AI content claims tailoring can be completed 'in 2 minutes,' while a separate offer markets paid manual applications and tailoring, suggesting competing automation-heavy and labor-heavy workflows rather than a settled approach.
The Glassdoor evidence is labeled 2026-08-04, but the quoted review text says June 8, 2020, creating a recency mismatch.
